facts: Rachel Smolker, Andrew Richards, Richard Connor, Janet Mann, and Per Berggren published the study in Ethology in June 1997.
The paper investigates whether sponge carrying on the rostra of bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops sp.) in Shark Bay, Western Australia, represents a foraging specialization involving tool use.
The sponges carried by the dolphins were identified as Echinodictyum mesenterinum.
Five regularly sighted individuals carried sponges in 67–100% of encounters, and all five were female.
Four other regularly sighted individuals carried sponges only once (two females, one likely female, one male).
Sponge carrying occurred mostly in a restricted deep-water channel measuring 8–10 meters deep.
Focal and surface observations revealed a stereotyped surfacing and diving pattern, along with occasional indications of prey consumption.
The authors evaluated three hypotheses (play, medicinal compounds, and foraging tool use), concluding that the foraging tool hypothesis was best supported.
